A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EEG-Language Modeling for Pathology Detection by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original EEG/report retrieval, TUAB linear-probe and zero-shot classification results, and experimental analyses in its appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds ELM-MIL experiments, NMT external validation, TUSZ/TUEV classification, and further ablations.

M1.justification: v3 introduces ELM-MIL alongside the retained ELM variants. It samples multiple positive EEG crops and report segments per subject and uses directional or bidirectional MIL-InfoNCE alignment, substantially changing the training objective and pairing procedure while retaining the EEG backbone.

E1.justification: TUEG pretraining and the original TUAB and retrieval coverage are retained. v3 adds external abnormality classification on NMT, seizure/background classification on TUSZ, and six-class event classification on TUEV, extending both population coverage and clinical task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds an identical-backbone supervised baseline to TUAB comparisons and evaluates it on TUSZ/TUEV. Table 4 additionally compares published results for SPaRCNet, CNN-Transformer, FFCL, ST-Transformer, BIOT, CEReBrO, and LaBraM variants. These literature comparisons use differing data and architectures; they are not documented as controlled reruns.

E3.justification: New protocols include five-fold TUSZ/TUEV evaluation, five-second pretraining with task-specific learning rates and subject exclusions, and ten-second crop-level TUAB evaluation using 80% labels. NMT uses its supplied train/test split. These extend the original recording-level evaluation; the retained 20/60-second EEG-only/EEG-language settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds MIL aggregation and positive-sample-count ablations, comparative temperature sensitivity, TUEV per-class analysis, and subject-clustering visualizations across temperatures. The original shuffled-report, pretraining-overlap, crop-length, language-encoder, and prompt-sensitivity analyses are retained, sometimes relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The retained principal comparisons still report means and standard deviations over five training runs. The original three-seed temperature study and five-seed overlap analysis also remain. Additional results do not establish an increased run count for retained experiments or introduce confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new methods and tasks, including bidirectional ELM-MIL TUAB balanced accuracy of 87.11% and NMT AUROC of 89.77%, both at 100% labels. All six retained EEG-only TUAB rows are numerically unchanged. Original top-3 retrieval results and numerous text-specific classification entries are omitted when the earlier detailed comparisons are condensed.

T1.justification: Section 3.1.1 adds formal positive-index sets, modality-specific batch definitions, and the multi-positive objectives in Equations 10–13. The new formulation relaxes individual-pair alignment through aggregation over positive instances and normalization for varying instance counts. This substantially extends the mathematical formulation, although no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds report-content selection, contrastive alignment, and label-efficient pathology detection. v3 makes MIL-based handling of EEG/text misalignment a central contribution and broadens its main claims to four clinical evaluations, external generalization, and effective learning with a compact, inexpensive EEG encoder.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting selective MIL alignment and temperature-dependent subject clustering to performance. Appendix A.1 identifies reduced artifact/eye-movement sensitivity as a possible consequence of excluded report content. The discussion shifts from untested downstream generalization toward external-validation findings and scaling limitations, while omitting some earlier explanations and caveats about LLM-summary instability and dataset balancing.

D1.justification: v3 supplies MIL sampling and learning-rate settings and detailed supervised-baseline architecture, optimization, dropout, and stopping rules. It changes the reported CUDA version from 12.3 to 11.3. Most existing encoder, preprocessing, augmentation, and data-access information is retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds an EEG multiple-instance-learning discussion and explicitly connects its method to video-text MIL-NCE and attention-based MIL. It also positions compact ELMs against large EEG foundation models through reported comparisons. The earlier ECG-language discussion is condensed and several associated citations are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and discussion undergo substantial rewriting. Results previously embedded within Methods become a dedicated Experimental Results section with pretraining, baseline, and ablation subsections. Preprocessing and several analyses move into reorganized appendices, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. Figure 1 is redrawn around MIL, and Figure 2 combines retrieval and classification displays while removing the original top-3 panels. New benchmark and ablation tables, per-class plots, and embedding visualizations substantially expand the presentation; several existing appendix displays are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: NMT external validation and TUSZ/TUEV evaluations substantially address v2's explicitly acknowledged gaps in downstream generalization and pathology-specific testing. MIL ablations strengthen the evidence for the proposed alignment strategy, while per-class analysis exposes a meaningful applicability limitation. Some original detailed results are lost, and Table 4's differing architectures and pretraining data limit causal comparisons, but the added direct validation provides a substantial overall quality gain.
